text: Repeated feedback, matched performance, and path-dependent under-reliance

text: This paper studies how feedback reshapes reliance calibration after local AI failures.

text: Belief and feedback  ->  reliance calibration  ->  later action thresholds

text:
This is the second paper in the dissertation. The focus is not generic trust, but how reliance on AI is recalibrated through repeated feedback.
The paper sits between belief formation and downstream responsibility. It asks what happens after local failures enter the learning process.
So the object here is dynamic reliance, not one-shot adoption.

name: title
text: The puzzle is not whether people dislike errors, but how later reliance recovers
textPreview: The puzzle is not whether people dislike errors, but how later reliance recovers

name: subtitle
text: A single miss can matter differently when it is read as a problem of source quality rather than a temporary local mistake.
textPreview: A single miss can matter differently when it is read as a problem of source quality rather than a temporary local mistake.

text:
Imagine a repeated monitoring task in which you can keep your own judgment or accept AI assistance.
After each round, you learn whether your own judgment and the AI would have produced better outcomes.
The key issue is not the first reaction to one miss, but whether later reliance returns once performance normalizes.
textPreview: Imagine a repeated monitoring task in which you can keep your own judgment or accept AI assistance. | After each round, you learn whether...

text:
The same local error may be interpreted as evidence about the source itself: AI may feel systematically less trustworthy after a miss.
If that interpretation persists, later rounds are not just updated by fresh performance. They inherit the earlier shock.
The research puzzle is therefore path recovery, not simple error dislike.
textPreview: The same local error may be interpreted as evidence about the source itself: AI may feel systematically less trustworthy after a miss. | ...

text: Puzzle: when later performance is matched again, does reliance return symmetrically, or does an early AI miss leave a longer shadow?
textPreview: Puzzle: when later performance is matched again, does reliance return symmetrically, or does an early AI miss leave a longer shadow?

text:
I open with a repeated high-risk decision situation rather than with theory. The practical question is simple: if AI misses early, do people go back once performance recovers?
That is different from asking whether people dislike errors in general. The real issue is whether the early miss changes the later path of reliance.
So the puzzle is dynamic recovery, not one-shot aversion.

text:
The literature already tells us a lot about immediate reactions to algorithms, advice, and automation.
But most of that work is still better at explaining one-shot adoption than repeated-feedback path updating.
That is why this paper is not simply another trust study. It asks what happens after the first reaction, across later rounds.

text:
This slide states the benchmark clearly. Under symmetric learning, a comparable miss should be treated as a comparable signal once average quality is matched.
So if AI errors generate a larger or more durable penalty, the interpretation cannot be just 'a mistake happened.' It becomes a source-specific inference.
That gives us a clean theoretical contrast for the experiment.

text:
The gap is not a vague claim that the topic is under-studied. It has two concrete parts.
First, most work is not truly multi-round, so it cannot reveal whether early failures change later paths. Second, most work does not isolate whether AI errors are treated as more diagnostic than comparable non-AI errors.
That is why I frame the paper as dynamic asymmetry under repeated feedback.

text:
The mechanism is intentionally simple. A local miss can become a calibration shock if it lowers source attractiveness and reduces later willingness to rely.
That gives us two mechanism dimensions to test: timing heterogeneity and source asymmetry.
The point is not to show EWA parameters on this slide. The point is to make the path logic intuitive before the design arrives.

Before showing the treatments, I explain why this prototype is the right kind of task.
The requirements are there to isolate dynamic reliance updating: repeated rounds, full feedback, matched quality, a task that remains meaningful, and an abstract standardized environment.
This page is doing identification work before we even show the condition map.

text:
I end with the expected shape rather than with a wall of methods. The visual path matters first: a shock lowers reliance, and the path does not fully come back even when later performance improves.
Only after establishing that visible path difference do I invoke the learning mechanism. That keeps the reduced-form identification in the lead.
So the contribution is to identify path-dependent under-reliance after AI errors under matched average quality.
